explanations.explanation: This neuron lights up on discourse‐level comparison or concession markers—words like “as,” “like,” or inverted auxiliaries in constructions such as “as … as,” “just as/just like,” “as long as,” and “not only does” that introduce parallels or emphatic subordinate clauses.
This neuron lights up on the leading subword of rare, multi-syllabic content words—especially proper names, brands or technical terms—i.e. the initial piece of a long, low-frequency token.

This feature is essentially a “hyphen‐connector” detector—it lights up on the “–” tokens that join words or numbers into compounds or ranges (e.g. “second-round,” “last-minute,” “half-finished,” “sixth-seeded,” etc.).
This neuron is firing on Title-Case or ALL-CAP words in headings/titles—i.e. tokens that appear as part of product, event or article titles and marketing‐style headlines.

This neuron detects recurring letter-string “chunks” that correspond to mid-word stems or roots—especially Latin/European morphemes and loanword segments—across many languages (e.g. “prof,” “ult,” “inte,” “com,” “compat,” etc.). It flags these common lexical roots wherever they appear.

This feature acts as a “continuation” detector for multi-word proper names and brands, firing strongly on the second (or tail) element of compound named entities (e.g. Hilfiger in Tommy Hilfiger, Gurley in Todd Gurley, Wide in World Wide Web, Mand / ela in Mandela, etc.).

This feature fires on numeric tokens that serve as structured metadata fields—most often four-digit years (and by extension other numeric IDs or codes) in document timestamps, citations or similar date/ID contexts.

This feature fires on structured alphanumeric “codes” and acronyms—especially hyphen-connected tokens and their neighbors—such as date ranges (1898-1923), party or district labels (D-CA), model numbers (F-150), visa categories (F-1), stock-exchange/ticker abbreviations (NYSE, ASX:APA), and multi-letter organization acronyms (IAEA, WLF). It marks the hyphens (and the adjoining uppercase letters or digits) that join these formal identifiers.

This neuron fires on hyphenated tokens that start with an uppercase letter or acronym—e.g. “F-1,” “X-ray,” “X-Mas,” “X-Men,” “S&P,” “A-O,” “F-Type” etc.—i.e. model codes, product names or acronyms of the form UppercaseSegment-Uppercase/number.

This neuron is basically an orthographic n-gram detector—it lights up on frequent internal letter sequences (e.g. “ann,” “err,” “amb,” “app,” “men,” “ur,” etc.) that show up across names and ordinary words.
